problem.title: Count High-Value Results by Kit Type
problem.prompt: You manage an at-home diagnostic test kit platform. Each `kit_type` record represents a diagnostic test category (vitamin panel, allergy screen, etc.). The `result_release` table records every time a patient's test results were released, including the `price_paid` for that specific test. Write a query that lists every kit type alongside the count of result releases where the patient paid MORE THAN $75. Some kit types may have had no high-value releases, or no releases at all; those kit types must still appear in the output with a count of 0. Return columns `kit_type_id`, `kit_name`, and `high_value_count`, ordered by `kit_type_id` ascending. The filter on price_paid belongs to the result_release table (the right side of the join); ensure your join structure keeps every kit_type row regardless of whether it has any qualifying result releases.
problem.schema_ddl: CREATE TABLE kit_type (kit_type_id INT PRIMARY KEY, kit_name VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE result_release (release_id INT PRIMARY KEY, kit_type_id INT NOT NULL, patient_email VARCHAR(100) NOT NULL, price_paid DECIMAL(10,2) NOT NULL, released_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL);
problem.example_input_data: INSERT INTO kit_type (kit_type_id, kit_name) VALUES (1, 'Vitamin D Panel'), (2, 'Allergy Screen'), (3, 'Thyroid Function'), (4, 'Lipid Panel'); INSERT INTO result_release (release_id, kit_type_id, patient_email, price_paid, released_at) VALUES (101, 1, 'alice@example.com', 89.99, '2024-01-15 10:00:00'), (102, 1, 'bob@example.com', 45.00, '2024-01-16 11:00:00'), (103, 2, 'carol@example.com', 120.00, '2024-02-01 09:30:00'), (104, 2, 'dave@example.com', 60.00, '2024-02-03 14:00:00'), (105, 3, 'eve@example.com', 50.00, '2024-03-10 08:00:00'), (106, 3, 'frank@example.com', 55.00, '2024-03-12 16:00:00');

composite_moves: right-side numeric filter (price_paid > 75) placed in ON to keep all kit_types
COUNT(result_release.release_id) counts qualifying releases; returns 0 for non-matching kit types

hints: You need to preserve every kit type row, even those with no qualifying result releases. Consider which join type guarantees that.
The price_paid filter applies to the result_release table (the right side). Where you place that filter determines whether non-matching kit types appear in the output or silently disappear.
Place the price_paid > 75 condition in the ON clause alongside the join key, then COUNT(r.release_id) and GROUP BY the kit_type fields. COUNT of a right-table column returns 0 when no rows match.
problem.answer_key: SELECT kt.kit_type_id, kt.kit_name, COUNT(r.release_id) AS high_value_count FROM kit_type kt LEFT JOIN result_release r ON kt.kit_type_id = r.kit_type_id AND r.price_paid > 75 GROUP BY kt.kit_type_id, kt.kit_name ORDER BY kt.kit_type_id;

_meta.scenario: an at-home diagnostic test kit platform tracking kit shipped and results released

user_solution:
/*
Write a query that lists every kit type alongside the count of result releases where the patient paid MORE THAN $75.
Some kit types may have had no high-value releases, or no releases at all; those kit types must still appear in the output with a count of 0.
Return columns `kit_type_id`, `kit_name`, and `high_value_count`, ordered by `kit_type_id` ascending.
*/
SELECT
    k.kit_type_id,
    k.kit_name,
    SUM(CASE WHEN r.price_paid > 75 THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) AS high_value_count
FROM kit_type AS k
LEFT JOIN result_release AS r
ON k.kit_type_id = r.kit_type_id
GROUP BY 1, 2
ORDER BY 1;
